summary: Explains how Dublin Core metadata, a small set of elements for describing information resources, can be expressed using the META and LINK tags of HTML. This is an informational memo, and it was replaced by RFC 5791.

eli5.summary: Dublin Core is a set of labels like title and author. This shows how to hide those labels in a web page so search tools can read them.

questions: how to put dublin core metadata in html
how to add dublin core metadata to html
subtitle: How to embed Dublin Core metadata labels in HTML pages so search tools can find them.

tldr.problem: Search engines and indexing tools need to understand what a web page is about, when it was created, who wrote it, and other metadata. Metadata was scattered in different formats, making it hard to build tools that could extract and use it.
tldr.mechanism: Dublin Core is a small set of metadata elements (like Title, Creator, Date, Subject) designed to describe information resources. This RFC explains how to encode Dublin Core elements using the HTML META and LINK tags, so metadata travels inside HTML documents and search tools can easily extract it.
tldr.outcome: Web pages can embed consistent, machine-readable descriptions of themselves, allowing indexing software and harvesters to extract, process, and display that metadata. This RFC was replaced by RFC 5791.

today: RFC 2731 is an Informational RFC published in December 1999 explaining how to encode Dublin Core metadata in HTML 4.0. It was replaced by RFC 5791, which updated the encoding specification.

sections.title: Dublin Core and Metadata in HTML
sections.content:
The Dublin Core is a small set of metadata elements for describing information resources. Metadata is data about data—information that describes the resource itself rather than its content. Examples include the title of a document, the person who created it, the date it was published, and keywords that describe its subject.

This RFC explains how to express Dublin Core elements using standard HTML 4.0 META and LINK tags so that metadata can be embedded directly in HTML documents. When a web page contains embedded Dublin Core metadata, indexing tools, harvesters, and search software can extract that description, catalog the page, and make it discoverable. The RFC shows how to encode elements, define namespaces with LINK tags, qualify elements with schemes and languages, and includes practical Perl scripts for extracting and automating metadata creation.
sections.eli5: Web pages are like books without labels. This shows how to add invisible labels—title, author, date—inside the HTML so a computer reading the page can understand what it is.

sections.title: The META Tag Format
sections.content:
The HTML META tag is designed to encode a named metadata element. The basic format is:

<meta name="PREFIX.ELEMENT_NAME" content="ELEMENT_VALUE">

For Dublin Core elements, the PREFIX is DC, so a creator would be encoded as <meta name="DC.Creator" content="Simpson, Homer">. Multiple META tags with the same name can appear (for example, multiple authors), and they can appear in any order. Each DC element is optional. Within the tag, the first letter of the Dublin Core element name is capitalized (Creator, not creator). Multiple META tags may appear together with different element names.

Non-Dublin-Core elements use other prefixes (such as AC for A-Core elements), allowing Dublin Core metadata to be interspersed with other metadata types. Special characters in element values can be encoded as HTML character entity references (such as é for an accented e).
sections.eli5: You write <meta name="DC.Title" content="My Page"> to label the page title. The DC means Dublin Core. You can have many labels, and they don't have to be in any order.

sections.title: Defining Namespaces with LINK and Qualifiers
sections.content:
The LINK tag associates a prefix with a URL that defines the element set. A complete metadata block includes one LINK tag for each prefix used. The LINK tag tells processors where to find the definition of the DC namespace. When multiple element sets are mixed, each must have its own schema LINK.

Dublin Core elements can be qualified to add nuance. Three types of qualifiers are used: the lang attribute specifies the language of the metadata content (not the resource), the scheme attribute identifies a controlled vocabulary or format (such as RFC1766 for language codes), and subelement names extend element names (such as DC.Date.Created for the creation date versus DC.Date.Available). These qualifiers allow metadata to describe multilingual resources, cite sources using standard schemes, and capture specific types of metadata within a general category.
sections.eli5: The LINK tag says where to find the definition of the DC labels. Qualifiers are extra notes: lang="es" says the content is in Spanish, scheme="RFC1766" says the value follows a standard format, and DC.Date.Created distinguishes when it was made from when it became available.

sections.title: The Dublin Core Element Set
sections.content:
The Dublin Core includes 15 core elements for describing resources: Title (name given to the resource), Creator (entity that created the content), Subject (topic or keyword), Description (account, summary, or abstract), Publisher (entity that made it available), Contributor (other entity that contributed), Date (event in the resource's life), Type (nature, genre, or category), Format (physical or digital data format), Identifier (unique identifier of the resource), Source (reference to the resource's origin), Language (language of the content), Relation (reference to related resources), Coverage (extent or scope of the content), and Rights (rights management or copyright information).

Each element can appear multiple times, be qualified with schemes and languages, and use subelements. For example, a book might have multiple creators (editors, photographers, illustrators), multiple dates (created, published, available), and multiple languages for title and description in different versions.
sections.eli5: Dublin Core has 15 basic labels: title, author, date, subject, description, and so on. You pick the ones you need for your page. Each label can appear many times and have extra notes about language or format.

sections.title: Recommended Encoding Style
sections.content:
While HTML allows many variations in META tag syntax, the RFC recommends a consistent encoding style to encourage easy development of metadata extraction and processing software. Recommendations include: capitalizing the first letter of Dublin Core element names, using double quotes around attribute values, placing one META tag per line, and adhering to consistent spacing.

Following these conventions ensures compatibility with popular freely available metadata indexing and manipulation tools such as SWISH-E, freeWAIS, Glimpse, Harvest, and Isearch, as well as with the Perl metadata processing scripts included in the RFC. Ordering of metadata elements is not preserved in general, so software should try to preserve relative ordering of elements with the same name (such as multiple authors) but users have no guarantee of this. Software support for qualifiers and LINK tags for schema definitions is not yet widespread, but following recommendations ensures future compatibility.
sections.eli5: To make your metadata work with tools, follow a consistent style: capitalize element names, use quotes, put each label on its own line. This way harvesting tools know what to expect.

viz.caption: A complete HTML page with Dublin Core metadata

data.title: Example from RFC 2731
data.code:
<html>
<head>
<title>A Dirge</title>
<link rel="schema.DC" href="http://purl.org/DC/elements/1.0/">
<meta name="DC.Title" content="A Dirge">
<meta name="DC.Creator" content="Shelley, Percy Bysshe">
<meta name="DC.Type" content="poem">
<meta name="DC.Date" content="1820">
<meta name="DC.Format" content="text/html">
<meta name="DC.Language" content="en">
</head>
<body>
Rough wind, that moanest loud
Grief too sad for song...
</body>
</html>
